pages.text:
Challenge Brief: The Autonomous Hospital Receptionist

Background
Hospitals lose patient time, staff capacity, and revenue because the patient journey is fragmented across
phone calls, front-desk queues, appointment systems, WhatsApp messages, billing desks, and follow-up
calls. Front-desk teams handle high call volumes, repetitive scheduling requests, insurance and
report-status queries, and no-show recovery, while urgent patient needs can be delayed behind routine
administrative work.

Your startup’s AI receptionist can answer calls and support patients from their first interaction through the
end of their hospital journey. The challenge is to turn that capability into a reliable, safe, and
production-ready patient-journey orchestration system.

The Challenge
Build a voice-first AI hospital receptionist that manages a patient’s end-to-end journey—from the first
inbound call to post-visit follow-up—while safely escalating clinical risk and handing off to hospital staff
when needed.

Your solution should not be a generic chatbot or a simple appointment-booking IVR. It should act as an
intelligent operations layer for the hospital: understanding the patient’s intent, maintaining context across
the journey, taking actions in hospital systems, coordinating communications, and escalating
appropriately.

Patient Journey to Support
Teams must demonstrate a working journey across at least the following stages:
• Inbound call handling: Answer a patient call naturally, identify intent, handle interruptions and follow-up
questions, and determine whether the request is administrative, logistical, or potentially urgent.
• Patient identification and registration: Match an existing patient using safe verification steps, or guide a
new patient through registration while preventing duplicate records and capturing only necessary
information.
• Pre-visit intake: Collect a structured reason for visit, symptoms, duration, severity, medications,
allergies, insurance details, preferred language, and accessibility needs where relevant.
• Appointment orchestration: Check doctor, department, location, and slot availability; book, reschedule,
cancel, or waitlist appointments according to hospital rules and patient constraints.
• Pre-visit preparation: Send confirmations and reminders, provide preparation instructions, request
required documents, answer directions and visiting-hours questions, and reduce avoidable no-shows.
• In-hospital coordination: Support check-in status, queue updates, department navigation, test
preparation, and status queries during the visit.
• Post-visit follow-up: Send follow-up instructions, collect feedback, schedule follow-up appointments,
answer report-status questions, and identify patients who need outreach.
• Clinical-risk escalation: Detect urgent symptoms, distressed callers, or situations outside the agent’s
scope, then immediately transfer to a triage nurse, emergency workflow, or appropriate staff member
with a concise context summary.

What You Must Build
Your submission should include:
• A live voice interface capable of handling a realistic multi-turn patient call.
• Streaming speech recognition, natural turn-taking, interruption handling, and natural voice response.

• A persistent patient-journey state machine that tracks the patient across the full workflow.
• Tool integrations or realistic mock APIs for scheduling, patient records, department availability,
notifications, queue status, billing/report status, and staff escalation.
• Retrieval grounded in approved hospital knowledge sources for policies, departments, doctors,
procedures, preparation instructions, and frequently asked questions.
• A clinical-safety and escalation layer that prevents diagnosis, treatment advice, or unsafe autonomous
decisions.
• A human handoff mechanism with a concise call summary, collected data, urgency level, and reason
for escalation.
• Multilingual support: English plus at least one Indian language. Hindi-English code-switching is
strongly encouraged.
• A supervisor dashboard showing live calls, conversation state, extracted information, tool calls,
escalation alerts, and audit history.
• An evaluation suite with at least 50 test scenarios, including routine bookings, incomplete information,
angry or confused callers, ambiguous symptoms, emergency red flags, rescheduling, and attempts to
obtain sensitive data.

Core User Stories
• As a patient, I can call the hospital at any time and have my request understood without navigating a
rigid IVR menu.
• As a new patient, I can register and book an appointment through a guided conversation.
• As a returning patient, I can reschedule or cancel an appointment without waiting for a human agent.
• As a patient, I can receive reminders, directions, preparation instructions, and document requests
before my visit.
• As a patient, I can ask about my appointment, report status, bill, department, or visiting hours and
receive a grounded answer.
• As a patient with urgent symptoms, I must be immediately connected to an appropriate human with full
context.
• As a front-desk staff member, I can see live calls, intervene when needed, and receive a clear
summary before taking over.
• As a hospital administrator, I can see call volume, booking outcomes, escalations, no-show risks, and
workflow bottlenecks.

Safety Requirements
The solution must be designed as a hospital operations assistant, not a medical decision-making system.
• Do not diagnose conditions or recommend treatment.
• Do not provide clinical advice beyond approved scripts and hospital policies.
• Escalate immediately when symptoms, context, or caller distress suggest urgency.
• Use only approved hospital knowledge sources; do not generate unsupported medical or policy
information.
• Minimize sensitive data exposure in logs, transcripts, dashboards, and notifications.
• Maintain an audit trail for identity verification, consent, data access, tool actions, escalations, and
appointment changes.
• Always provide an immediate, obvious path to a human staff member.

Technical Constraints
• The primary interface must be voice; SMS, WhatsApp, web, or dashboard interfaces may supplement
it.
• The system must maintain conversational state across multiple calls or channels where feasible.
• The solution should be designed for real-time interaction, with a clearly measured latency budget.
• Teams may use mock hospital systems, but the integrations must be realistic and clearly documented.
• Teams must show how the system behaves when a tool fails, data is incomplete, or the patient
changes topic.
• Teams must disclose which components use AI models, which rules are deterministic, and where
human oversight is required.

Deliverables
By the end of the challenge, each team must submit:
• A working end-to-end prototype.
• A live or recorded demo covering at least three patient journeys: new-patient registration and
appointment booking; returning-patient rescheduling and pre-visit preparation; and urgent-symptom
detection and safe escalation.
• A supervisor/staff dashboard.
• A system architecture diagram showing the voice pipeline, agent orchestration, tools, data stores, and
escalation path.
• An evaluation report with test scenarios, success rate, escalation accuracy, latency, and failure cases.
• A short product brief explaining the target hospital user, workflow, deployment model, and path to
production.

Judging Criteria
End-to-end journey completion — 25%: Ability to complete registration, intake, scheduling, preparation,
and follow-up workflows.

Conversation quality — 20%: Natural interaction, interruption handling, clarification, memory, and
multilingual support.

Safety and escalation — 20%: Red-flag detection, appropriate boundaries, human handoff, and
auditability.

System integration — 15%: Realistic tool use, state consistency, scheduling accuracy, and recovery from
failures.

Reliability and grounding — 10%: Handling of incomplete data, errors, unknown questions, and
hallucination prevention.

Product experience — 10%: Supervisor dashboard, usability, accessibility, deployment readiness, and
demo quality.

Winning Solution
The winning team will demonstrate an AI receptionist that feels like a capable hospital front-desk
colleague: it completes real work, remembers context, coordinates systems, communicates clearly, knows
its limits, and escalates safely when a patient needs a human.
